subject: forensic-medicine
title: Identification: Tattoo Marks, Mutilation and DNA Fingerprinting

steps.title: Tattoo pigments and biological dermis deposition
steps.tx: In forensic identification, a permanent **tattoo mark indelible design** is created by puncturing the epidermis with needles and introducing insoluble pigments into the vascular reticular dermis. While epidermal cellular layers shed continuously, dermal macrophages phagocytose the pigment particles, trapping them permanently within dermal collagen bundles. Even when the epidermis macerates during postmortem drowning or putrefaction, the deeper dermal tattoo design remains visible.
steps.say: Tattoos are permanent because ink particles are trapped by dermal macrophages in the deep skin, remaining visible even when outer skin peels away.

steps.title: Medicolegal significance and regional lymph node migration
steps.tx: The discovery of tattoos provides crucial clues to personal identity, reflecting names, religious symbols, military emblems, gang affiliations, or prison histories. Crucially, when criminals attempt surgical excision or skin peels during decomposition, the **lymphatic tattoo pigment migration** phenomenon assists identification: phagocytosed pigment particles drain into regional lymph nodes (e.g. axillary or inguinal nodes), tattooing the nodal cortex black or blue on autopsy dissection.
steps.say: Tattoos reveal names, religion, and military history. When skin is destroyed, ink draining into regional lymph nodes confirms tattooing on autopsy.

steps.title: Removal techniques and residual cicatricial scarring
steps.tx: Individuals frequently attempt **tattoo mark deliberate removal** to disguise identity or eliminate gang emblems. Conventional methods include surgical excision, dermabrasion, chemical cautery with salabrasion or trichloroacetic acid, and modern Q-switched Nd:YAG laser photothermolysis. However, surgical and chemical removal methods leave distinct telltale cicatricial scars that preserve the original outline, which can be visualized under oblique lighting or ultraviolet photography.
steps.say: Removing tattoos with surgery, acids, or lasers leaves characteristic scars matching the original outline, detectable under special lighting.

steps.title: Criminal mutilation and dismemberment of corpses
steps.tx: In homicide investigations, perpetrators often commit **criminal mutilation of corpses** to obstruct victim identification and hinder transport. Dismemberment involves decapitation, amputating hands and feet to eliminate fingerprints, shaving pubic hair, burning facial features, or immersing remains in corrosive sulfuric acid. The forensic pathologist must assemble body fragments anatomically, match severed cut margins, reconstruct stature, and harvest deep bone for DNA testing.
steps.say: Perpetrators mutilate corpses by removing heads, hands, or facial skin to destroy identity, requiring pathologists to reassemble parts and sample bone for DNA.

steps.title: History and principles of DNA fingerprinting
steps.tx: Revolutionizing forensic jurisprudence, the **DNA profiling identification principle** was invented by Sir Alec Jeffreys in 1984, and pioneered in India by Dr. Lalji Singh at the Centre for DNA Fingerprinting and Diagnostics. Over ninety-nine percent of human DNA is identical across individuals; however, polymorphic non-coding regions exhibit hypervariable repeating sequence motifs known as Short Tandem Repeats (STRs) that provide unique genetic signatures.
steps.say: DNA profiling, invented by Alec Jeffreys, analyzes hypervariable short tandem repeat sequences in non-coding DNA to create unique genetic profiles.

rows: Developed Bkm-derived probe; established CDFD Hyderabad

steps.title: Biological sources of forensic DNA evidence
steps.tx: In criminal casework, forensic biologists isolate high-molecular-weight genomic material from diverse **biological specimens for DNA extraction**. Viable sources include peripheral bloodstains, seminal fluid, vaginal swabs, saliva on cigarette butts, hair shafts possessing nucleated follicular root sheaths, touched items containing epithelial skin flakes, tooth dental pulp, and deep compact cortical bone harvested from femoral shafts in skeletonized remains.
steps.say: DNA can be extracted from blood, semen, saliva, hair with roots, skin cells, dental pulp, and dense leg bone in skeletonized remains.

steps.tx: Peaks on an STR electropherogram come from multiplex PCR, each spike marking an allele length at a short tandem repeat locus. Those profiles are built from **biological specimens for DNA extraction** such as bloodstains, semen, vaginal swabs, saliva left on a cigarette, hairs that still have a root sheath, shed skin, tooth pulp, and dense cortex taken from a femoral shaft. Bare shafts without nuclei are a poor source.

steps.tx: Casework profiles begin with **biological specimens for DNA extraction** that still hold high molecular weight genomic material. Useful sources include bloodstains, seminal fluid, vaginal swabs, saliva on cigarette butts, hairs that keep a nucleated root sheath, skin flakes on touched objects, dental pulp, and compact cortical bone from the femoral shaft of skeletonised remains. The electropherogram peaks are only as informative as the specimen that supplied that DNA.
steps.say: Short tandem repeat peaks are read from DNA taken from blood, semen, vaginal swabs, saliva, rooted hairs, skin flakes, tooth pulp, or dense femoral bone when the body is only a skeleton.

steps.title: Short Tandem Repeat analysis and multiplex PCR
steps.tx: Modern casework utilizes **Short Tandem Repeat multiplex amplification**, targeting repeating tetranucleotide or pentanucleotide motifs across twenty standardized chromosomal loci. Forensic geneticists amplify these micro-loci simultaneously using multiplex polymerase chain reaction tagged with fluorescent dyes. Capillary electrophoresis separates the amplified DNA fragments by base-pair length, generating an electropherogram showing distinct allele peaks with match probabilities exceeding one in billions.
steps.say: Forensic labs amplify twenty short tandem repeat markers using multiplex PCR and capillary electrophoresis, yielding match probabilities over one in a billion.

steps.title: Y-chromosome STR profiling in sexual assault
steps.tx: When analyzing sexual assault specimens containing overwhelming amounts of female victim epithelial cells mixed with minute quantities of male semen, **Y-chromosome STR lineage testing** provides an invaluable diagnostic solution. Because primers target only the male-specific Y-chromosome non-recombining region, the female background DNA does not amplify, allowing unhindered profiling of the male perpetrator and determining the number of male contributors in gang rape.
steps.say: Y-STR testing targets only male DNA, allowing detectives to detect male rapist semen mixed with overwhelming female cells in sexual assault samples.

steps.title: Mitochondrial DNA analysis in charred and degraded remains
steps.tx: When severe thermal charring, advanced putrefaction, or weathered skeletonization degrades nuclear DNA, forensic scientists deploy **mitochondrial DNA hypervariable sequencing**. Because each human cell contains hundreds of mitochondria carrying circular double-stranded DNA genomes, mtDNA survives extreme environmental insults. Sequenced across hypervariable control regions (HV1 and HV2), mtDNA is inherited strictly through maternal lineage, enabling identification using distant maternal relatives.
steps.say: Mitochondrial DNA survives extreme heat and decay because hundreds of copies exist per cell. Inherited maternally, it matches charred remains to maternal family.
